questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What port-based access control removes
questions.learningObjective: Identify what port-based access control removes from the exposure.
questions.stem: Sheet 4 of the survey plot asks what a switch that learns which devices may use each port removes from the picture.

options.text: It removes the chance that an unauthorised device is plugged in and starts sending traffic
It removes the chance that traffic crossing the wire is read by a nearby observer
options.misconception: believes port control prevents passive interception of traffic

options.text: It removes the chance that a malicious program runs with the privileges of its user
options.misconception: thinks port control stops malicious programs running on a host

options.text: It removes the chance that a server on the network is reached by an unauthorised host
options.misconception: confuses restricting a port with restricting access to a server

questions.explanation: Port-based control limits which devices may use a given switch port, so an unauthorised device cannot simply be plugged in and join. It does not hide traffic on the wire or affect anything inside a host.
questions.hint: Ask what the switch can see and refuse at the socket.

questions.topic: What full-disk encryption does and does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Compare what full-disk encryption protects across two laptops.
questions.stem: Plate 7 of the field survey compares two laptops and asks what the protection installed on them actually covers.

options.text: Both protect data while running, but only the one with a chip protects data while powered off
options.misconception: assumes the powered-off case is only covered by special hardware

options.text: Both keep the drive unreadable, but neither protects data while the machine is unlocked and running
Only the laptop with hardware support resists offline reading of its drive contents
options.misconception: believes software encryption leaves the drive readable offline

options.text: Both hide everything from anyone who holds the machine but not the passphrase
options.misconception: thinks the disk stays unreadable to anyone holding the machine

questions.explanation: Full-disk encryption protects the contents of the drive, so pulling the disk and reading it directly yields nothing while it is locked. Once the machine is unlocked and running, the data is available to anything that gets execution on that host.

questions.stem: Legend entry 12 on the map records a recovery key written as 8 groups of 6 characters, and the vault keeps 3 paper copies of that key.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the measured boot chain establishes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a measured boot chain establishes about startup.
questions.stem: Border note 5 of the survey sheet asks for a written explanation of what a measured boot chain establishes about what ran at startup.

answer.exemplar: A measured boot chain records a digest of each stage as it executes, so the recorded values prove exactly which firmware, bootloader and kernel images ran on that machine at that boot. Because the measurements are compared against values sealed in trusted storage, a modified bootloader or a substituted kernel is detected before it can hand control to the next stage. What the chain establishes is the integrity of the early startup path, and it says nothing about what runs once the operating system is already in charge.

questions.explanation: Measuring each startup stage and sealing the expected values lets the machine detect a changed bootloader or kernel before running it. The guarantee covers the boot path only, and stops once the operating system takes over.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the startup the measurements actually cover.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a stack canary detects
questions.learningObjective: State what a failed stack canary check indicates.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the plotting sheet describes a function that stores a local guard value on the stack before a buffer is filled and checks it when the function returns. The note records that the check failed during one run and the program stopped immediately.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the plotting sheet, what does the failed check tell the surveyor?

options.text: That the program was compiled without the optimisation that removes the guard value
options.misconception: thinks the check failed because the compiler removed the guard

options.text: That the buffer was filled correctly but the guard value was stored at a fixed address
options.misconception: assumes the failure came from where the guard value was stored

options.text: That something wrote beyond the buffer and overwrote the guard value on the stack
That the function returned a wrong result even though no memory was written out of bounds
options.misconception: believes the failed check can happen without an out of bounds write

questions.explanation: The guard value sits between the buffer and the rest of the frame, so a write past the end of the buffer changes it. A mismatch therefore reports an out-of-bounds write, which is different from a wrong result with intact memory.
questions.hint: Ask what sits between the buffer and the rest of the frame.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What non-executable memory changes about a code-reuse attempt
questions.learningObjective: State what non-executable memory does to a code-reuse attempt.
questions.stem: Grid square C4 of the plotting sheet asks for two facts about code that tries to run injected instructions from a data buffer.

options.text: It cannot execute the injected bytes, and the injected instructions run inside the calling function
options.misconception: believes the injected code falls back to running inside the caller

options.text: It cannot execute the injected bytes, and the attempt usually ends with the program being stopped
It executes the injected bytes only if they are aligned to an instruction boundary
options.misconception: thinks alignment of the injected bytes makes them executable

options.text: It executes the injected bytes, and the program continues as if nothing had happened
options.misconception: assumes the buffer is executable and the injection simply works

questions.explanation: Marking the data region as non-executable means the processor refuses to fetch instructions from it, so the injected bytes stay data. The refusal is usually fatal to the process, so the attack ends there.
questions.hint: Ask what the processor is allowed to do with that memory.

questions.topic: A host rule set that keys a program by its path
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a path-keyed host rule set protects.
questions.stem: The projection legend for the west block asks what a host rule set that allows a program only at one path actually protects.

options.text: It stops the allowed program from being modified after it has been installed
options.misconception: believes a path rule protects the installed file from modification

options.text: It stops the allowed program from reading files outside its own working directory
options.misconception: thinks a path rule restricts which files the program may open

options.text: It stops any user other than the owner from running the allowed program at all
options.misconception: assumes a path rule limits which users may run the program

options.text: It stops a different program with the same name from being launched in place of the allowed one

questions.explanation: A path rule identifies the program by where it sits, so a copy placed elsewhere does not inherit the permission. It says nothing about modification of the file, file access by the program, or which users may run it.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a switch table whose entries came from a single port.
questions.stem: Survey marker 9 on the map records a switch table with 6 entries, all learned from the same port on the uplink.

options.text: Every entry was learned from one port, so a device on that port could claim any of the addresses
Every entry was learned from one port, so no other device on the network could send traffic
options.misconception: thinks one source port blocks every other device from sending

options.text: Every entry was learned from one port, so the switch has not yet learned the uplink address
options.misconception: assumes the uplink address is missing from the table

options.misconception: believes learning from one port fills the table permanently

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What full-disk encryption does and does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain what full-disk encryption protects and what it leaves out.
questions.stem: Scale note 8 of the drawing asks for a written explanation of what full-disk encryption protects and what it leaves out.

answer.exemplar: Full-disk encryption protects the contents of the storage device while it is locked, so a removed drive, a stolen laptop or a discarded disk yields nothing without the key. It does not protect a machine that has already been unlocked, because the data is then available in ordinary memory to any program that runs on it, and it does not protect the network traffic or the account that was used to unlock the machine.

questions.explanation: The protection applies to the device while it is locked, which covers theft and disposal. Once the machine is unlocked the data is ordinary readable memory, and network traffic is untouched by it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the machine is locked when the disk is read.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where the recovery key changes the answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a written copy of a recovery key changes its protection.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the survey sheet describes a recovery key that is held by a small team and used when the normal unlock credentials are lost. The note records that the key was also written on a card in a drawer in the same office.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the survey sheet, what does the card in the drawer change about the recovery key?

options.text: It has no effect, because the key still needs the presence of a named team member
options.misconception: believes the presence of a named person protects a written copy

options.text: It shortens the key lifetime, because the card must be replaced at every rotation
options.misconception: thinks a written copy shortens the rotation interval

options.text: It strengthens the key, because a second copy gives a fallback when the primary is lost
options.misconception: assumes a second copy of the key improves its protection

options.text: It removes most of the value of the key, because anyone who reaches the drawer can recover full access

questions.explanation: A written copy in the same place as the machine removes the protection that separation was meant to provide, because whoever reaches the drawer gets the full key. Only the recovery process itself is protected, not the stored material.
questions.hint: Ask what separation was supposed to achieve.

options.misconception: thinks the measurement covers later compromise of the system

options.text: It can prove which early startup images ran, and it cannot prove what ran after the operating system started
It can prove the machine has never been compromised, and it cannot prove which images ran at startup
options.misconception: overstates the guarantee into a claim of never being compromised

options.text: It can prove which early startup images ran, and it cannot prove anything about the hardware beneath them
options.misconception: believes the measurement cannot address the startup images

questions.explanation: The measurements cover the firmware, bootloader and kernel stages, so they establish which images ran at startup. They stop there and say nothing about what the running operating system does afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask how far along the startup path the guarantee reaches.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a stack canary detects
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a stack canary is designed to detect.
questions.stem: Legend entry 13 on the map asks what a stack canary is intended to detect during a normal run of a program.

options.text: A read that runs past the end of a buffer without changing any memory
options.misconception: believes the canary detects an over-read of a stack buffer

options.text: A write that runs past the end of a buffer while it is still on the heap
options.misconception: thinks the canary covers heap buffers

options.text: A write that runs past the end of a buffer and into the rest of the stack frame
A write that changes a value on the stack long after the function has returned
options.misconception: assumes the canary catches later changes to stack values

questions.explanation: The guard value is placed at the edge of the stack frame, so an overlong write into the frame changes it and the check fails. It targets stack overflows, not heap overflows and not over-reads.
questions.hint: Ask where the guard value is placed relative to the buffer.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What non-executable memory changes about a code-reuse attempt
questions.learningObjective: Compare a run with executable data regions and one without.
questions.stem: Border note 14 of the survey sheet compares a run with executable data regions and one with them marked non-executable.

options.text: In the first run the program stopped, and in the second run the injected bytes were silently discarded
options.misconception: reverses the behaviour of the two runs

options.text: In the first run the injected instructions executed, and in the second run the program stopped instead
In both runs the injected instructions executed, because the marker only applies to new allocations
options.misconception: assumes the marker does not affect existing memory regions

options.text: In both runs the program stopped, because the marker applies to every region at once
options.misconception: believes the marker changes the behaviour of the first run as well

questions.explanation: The marker changes what the processor will do with the memory, so the same injected bytes run in the first case and are refused in the second. In the refused case the process usually terminates.
questions.hint: Ask what the processor does differently in each run.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A switch that learns bindings from one source only
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a switch with bindings from one source only is unsafe.
questions.stem: The projection legend for the east block asks for a written explanation of why a switch that learns bindings from one source only is unsafe.

answer.exemplar: A switch builds its address table by watching the source address of arriving frames and recording the port they came in on. If every entry was learned from a single port, then a device plugged into that port can send frames with any of the recorded source addresses and the switch will forward traffic for those addresses to it. The switch cannot tell the real device from the impostor, because it never verified the addresses, it only observed them.

questions.explanation: Learning from source addresses means the switch trusts what it observes. With all bindings taken from one port, a device on that port can claim any of those addresses and the switch will forward to it.
questions.hint: Ask how the switch decides which port an address belongs to.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What port-based access control removes
questions.learningObjective: Identify which traffic a per-port device limit actually protects.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the plotting sheet describes a switch where 4 ports accept only a single authorised device address each and close when a different device appears. A second note records that the trunk port carrying traffic between switches is not covered by the rule.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the plotting sheet, which traffic does the rule on those 4 ports actually protect?

options.text: Only the traffic entering through those 4 ports, leaving the unprotected trunk outside the rule
All traffic on the site, because the switch checks every frame that passes through it
options.misconception: believes the rule covers every frame the switch handles

options.text: Only encrypted traffic, because unencrypted frames cannot be matched to a device address
options.misconception: thinks the rule only applies to encrypted traffic

options.text: Nothing at all, because a device address can be copied by an attacker on the same port
options.misconception: assumes a device address cannot be copied by anyone

questions.explanation: The rule is enforced per port where a frame enters, so it covers only the 4 ports it is configured on. The trunk and every other path are outside it, and copying an address is what the check catches.
questions.hint: Ask where in the path the rule is applied.

options.misconception: confuses disk protection with protection of network traffic

options.text: It protects the account used on a lost machine, and it does not protect data held in memory
options.misconception: believes encryption protects the login account itself

options.text: It protects data held in memory on a lost machine, and it does not protect the data on the drive
options.misconception: reverses which data the protection covers

options.text: It protects the drive of a lost machine, and not the data held in memory while it ran

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where the recovery key changes the answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a recovery key grants compared with ordinary credentials.
questions.stem: Contour annotation 18 of the chart asks what a recovery key changes compared with the ordinary credentials it replaces.

options.text: It grants limited access to a single file while leaving the rest of the drive locked
options.misconception: thinks a recovery key unlocks only a single file

options.text: It grants access only for a limited number of attempts before it is destroyed
options.misconception: assumes a recovery key expires after a fixed number of tries

options.text: It grants full access to the protected material without needing the normal unlock credential
It grants access only to the account of the person who created the recovery key
options.misconception: believes a recovery key is bound to one named account

questions.explanation: A recovery key is a substitute for the normal unlock credential, so it opens the protected material completely. That is what makes it worth protecting carefully, since possession of it bypasses the usual check.

The kernel row, whose recorded digest does not match the value sealed in trusted storage

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What non-executable memory changes about a code-reuse attempt
questions.learningObjective: Explain why non-executable memory defeats a code-reuse attempt.
questions.stem: Sheet 21 of the survey plot asks for a written explanation of why marking a data region as non-executable defeats a code-reuse attempt.

answer.exemplar: A code-reuse attempt places instructions where data belongs and then jumps to them, so the processor fetches and runs those bytes as if they were code. Marking that region as non-executable changes what the processor is permitted to do there: it may read and write the bytes as data, but a jump into the region raises a fault instead of transferring control. The injected bytes stay inert, and the process usually ends there instead of carrying the attack on.

questions.explanation: The attack works by getting the processor to execute data. Marking that memory non-executable removes the permission to fetch instructions from it, so the jump faults and the injected bytes never run.
questions.hint: Ask what permission the attack needs from the processor.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the survey sheet describes a rule set that permits a utility only when it is run from a fixed installation path, and denies it at every other location. A second note records that the same utility can be copied to a writable folder and run there.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the survey sheet, what happens when the utility is copied to a writable folder and run?

options.text: The rule set allows it, because the copied file is byte for byte the same program
options.misconception: believes identical content satisfies a rule written about a location

options.text: The rule set denies it, because the copy does not sit at the path the rule names
The rule set denies it and also removes the file that was copied, on the grounds it is unauthorised
options.misconception: assumes the rule set deletes files that fail the check

options.text: The rule set allows it, because the rule is checked against the contents of the file
options.misconception: thinks the rule is matched against the file contents

questions.explanation: The rule is written about a location, so the copy at a different path fails the match and is refused. Identity of content is irrelevant to the check, and refusing a program does not remove it from disk.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule names the program or the place.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the measured boot chain establishes
questions.learningObjective: Account for what a measured boot chain proves and what it cannot.
questions.stem: The projection legend for the north block asks for a written account of what a measured boot chain proves and what it cannot prove.

answer.exemplar: A measured boot chain digests each firmware and software image as it is loaded and compares the digest with a value that was sealed earlier, so it can show that the bootloader and the kernel that ran were the expected ones. It cannot show that the kernel was free of defects, that the operating system stayed uncompromised afterwards, or that the hardware beneath the platform was trustworthy, because none of those are covered by the measurements taken before the operating system takes control.

questions.explanation: The measurements prove which startup images ran, because each is checked against a sealed value before it executes. They say nothing about the kernel being sound or the hardware below.
questions.hint: Ask what is measured and when the measurement stops.

questions.topic: What a stack canary detects
questions.learningObjective: State what protection remains when a canary check is compiled out.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the plotting sheet records a program whose stack guard value is stored at the edge of the frame and verified on return. A note says that the program was built with the guard check compiled out by an optimisation setting, so the value is never examined.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the survey sheet, what protection remains in that program?

options.text: Full protection, because the guard value is still stored in the frame
options.misconception: believes storing the guard value alone provides the protection

options.text: Partial protection, because the write is still recorded somewhere in the frame
options.misconception: thinks the corrupted frame is itself a form of detection

options.text: Protection against overflow only, because the check runs at the end of the program
options.misconception: assumes the check runs once at the end of the program

options.text: None from the guard, because the value is never checked even when a write clobbers it

questions.explanation: The guard only works if it is compared, and a build that removes the comparison removes the protection entirely even though the value is still stored. Detection comes from the check, not from the bytes.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a guard that is never compared.

questions.topic: What non-executable memory changes about a code-reuse attempt
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of a non-executable region on injected instructions.
questions.stem: Survey marker 27 on the map asks for two facts about a program whose data region has been marked non-executable.

options.text: Instructions placed in that region cannot be run, and the program carries on ignoring the attempt
options.misconception: believes the program continues unaffected after the failed attempt

options.text: Instructions placed in that region can still be run, and the program carries on as before
options.misconception: assumes the marker does not prevent instructions from running

options.text: Instructions placed in that region cannot be run, and the program is normally stopped when it tries
Instructions placed in that region can still be run, and the program is normally stopped when it tries
options.misconception: mixes the wrong outcome with the wrong enforcement

questions.explanation: The marker removes the permission to execute instructions from that region, so the attempt fails. The failure is normally fatal to the process rather than something the program can ignore.
questions.hint: Ask what the processor permits and what follows the refusal.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What full-disk encryption does and does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain why full-disk encryption is described as protection at rest.
questions.stem: Sheet 31 of the survey plot asks for a written explanation of why full-disk encryption is described as protection at rest.

answer.exemplar: The encryption is applied to the data while it sits on the storage device, so the protection is tied to the device being locked rather than to a particular moment in time. That is why a drive removed from a powered-off machine, a stolen laptop, or a disk sent for disposal reveals nothing without the key, while a machine that is running and unlocked holds its data in ordinary memory where any program on it can reach it.

questions.explanation: The protection is a property of the data on the device while the device is locked, which covers theft and disposal. A running, unlocked machine holds readable data in memory, outside that property.
questions.hint: Ask what state of the machine the protection depends on.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where the recovery key changes the answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a chat entry affects the protection a recovery key provides.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the survey sheet describes a recovery key that is generated once, stored in a sealed envelope, and used when the ordinary credentials are lost. A note records that the key was also pasted into a shared team chat where several people can read the history.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the survey sheet, what does the chat entry do to the protection the recovery key provides?

options.text: It has no effect, because the key was already stored in a sealed envelope
options.misconception: believes a sealed copy makes a chat copy harmless

options.text: It shortens the life of the key, because the chat entry must be removed at the next rotation
options.misconception: thinks a chat copy shortens the rotation interval

options.text: It hands the key to everyone with access to that history, so possession no longer proves anything
It strengthens the record, because a second copy gives a fallback if the envelope is lost
options.misconception: assumes a second copy of the key improves its protection

questions.explanation: A recovery key is only as good as the control over every copy of it. A paste into a shared history gives it to everyone with access, so the sealed envelope no longer limits who can recover the data.
questions.hint: Ask who can now read a copy of the key.

questions.stem: Plate 32 of the field survey asks for two facts about a measured boot chain: what it checks, and where the check happens.

options.text: It checks each startup image against a sealed value, and the check happens before that image runs
It checks each startup image against a sealed value, and the check happens after that image has run
options.misconception: moves the check to after the image has already run

options.text: It checks the running operating system against a sealed value, and the check happens at shutdown
options.misconception: confuses the early startup images with the running operating system

options.text: It checks each startup image against a value stored on the disk, and the check happens before it runs
options.misconception: believes the sealed value is stored on the same disk being checked

questions.explanation: Each image is digested and compared with a value sealed in trusted storage, and that comparison happens before the image is allowed to execute. Sealing it outside the measured disk stops an attacker swapping both.
questions.hint: Ask whether the check comes before or after the code runs.

options.misconception: assumes the canary needs a skipped length check to be useful

options.text: It prevents the write from happening, rather than reporting it after the damage is done
options.misconception: thinks the canary stops the overflow before it happens

options.text: It detects a write that overflows the buffer even when the buffer is on the heap
options.misconception: believes the canary covers heap buffers as well

options.text: It detects a write that overflows the buffer even when the length check was written incorrectly

questions.explanation: The canary is an independent check on the frame, so it reports a corrupting write even if the length validation was skipped or wrong. It reports damage rather than preventing it.

options.text: On the marked host the program stopped at the injected jump, and on the other host it continued

options.misconception: believes the marker changes storage but not execution

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A switch that learns bindings from one source only
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a switch does with bindings learned from a single port.
questions.stem: Survey marker 40 on the map asks for a written explanation of what a switch does when it has learned a binding from a single port.

answer.exemplar: A switch records, for each address it sees, the port on which a frame carrying that source address arrived, and it then forwards traffic for that address out of that port. Learning everything from one port means the table points every one of those addresses at the same place, so a device attached there and sending frames with a source address copied from another machine will receive traffic that was never intended for it. The switch is not guessing wrongly; it is reporting what it was told.

questions.explanation: Forwarding follows the table, and every entry learned from one port points at that port. A device there can present a copied source address and the switch will deliver traffic for it as if genuine.
questions.hint: Ask what the table says and what a copied address changes.

options.misconception: believes the rule applies only to uplinks

options.text: The device is redirected to a separate quarantine network for unrecognised addresses

options.text: The device loses network access on that port until the authorised address returns or the rule changes
The device continues with reduced speed while the switch logs the unexpected address
options.misconception: thinks the port degrades the connection rather than closing it

questions.explanation: Closing the port removes the device access entirely rather than degrading it or moving it elsewhere, so the device is isolated until the listed address reappears or the rule changes.
questions.hint: Ask what the closed port removes for the attached device.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What non-executable memory changes about a code-reuse attempt
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limit that non-executable memory places on exploitation.
questions.stem: Plate 43 of the field survey asks for a written explanation of the limit that non-executable memory places on a code-reuse attempt.

answer.exemplar: Marking a region non-executable means the processor will refuse to treat the bytes there as instructions, so the injected code cannot be reached by any ordinary jump or return into the data area. The limit is specific: it does not stop the attacker from writing into that memory, from corrupting pointers that point elsewhere, or from redirecting control to code that is genuinely executable. It removes one route to execution rather than closing off exploitation in general.

questions.explanation: The marker blocks execution from the data area, not writing to it and not corruption elsewhere. It removes one path to running injected code, leaving other attacks untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what the marker refuses and what it still permits.

options.misconception: assumes the rule refuses the legitimate launch

options.misconception: believes the rule blocks the configured path as well

questions.explanation: The rule permits the launch because the path matches exactly, and a copy placed elsewhere would fail the same match and be refused. The rule is about the location at launch, not about installation.

questions.topic: Where the recovery key changes the answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain why storage arrangements for a recovery key matter.
questions.stem: Survey marker 47 on the map asks for a written explanation of why the storage arrangements for a recovery key matter as much as the key itself.

answer.exemplar: A recovery key is only as protected as the least protected copy of it. A key written in a notebook beside the machine, pasted into a shared chat, or handed to a single person who then leaves the organisation removes the point of having the key at all, because the ordinary credential it replaces becomes the weaker link. Splitting the key into shares, keeping them apart, and rotating them on a fixed schedule all exist to make sure that losing one copy does not mean losing the protection.

questions.explanation: Every copy of the key is a copy of the secret, so where those copies live and who can read them decides the real protection. The key protects the material only while its storage keeps it out of reach.

questions.topic: A host rule set that keys a program by its path
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a rule set when the files at named paths have been replaced.
questions.stem: Scale note 59 of the drawing records that a rule set names 9 program paths, and that 2 of the named programs were replaced with different files since the rule was written.

options.text: The 2 replacements inherit the permission because the rule names only the path
options.misconception: thinks a path rule says nothing about what is stored at the path

options.text: The rule set compares the contents of each file and so still accepts the 2 replacements
options.misconception: assumes the rule set inspects file contents

options.text: The 2 replacements no longer match the rule and would be refused when they run
The rule set is invalidated as a whole and stops permitting any of the 9 programs
options.misconception: believes one mismatch invalidates every other entry

questions.explanation: A path rule matches the location, so the replacements at those two paths no longer satisfy it and are refused when run. The other seven entries are unaffected, and contents were never inspected.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule looks at the path or the file.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A switch that learns bindings from one source only
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many bindings were learned outside the concentrated port.
questions.stem: Compass annotation 60 of the sheet records a switch with 16 learned address bindings, of which 11 came from one uplink port.
questions.explanation: Of the 16 bindings, 11 came from the single uplink port, so 16 minus 11 leaves 5 bindings learned elsewhere. Those 5 point at different ports and are not exposed by the concentration.
questions.hint: Subtract the uplink count from the total bindings.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What full-disk encryption does and does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain how full-disk encryption changes the outcome of a discarded drive.
questions.stem: Sheet 51 of the survey plot asks for a written explanation of how full-disk encryption changes the outcome of a discarded drive.

answer.exemplar: With the drive encrypted, a disk pulled out of a machine or thrown into a bin is a container of unreadable bytes until the key is applied, so the disposal decision that usually worries people becomes routine. The protection depends on the key, not on where the drive ends up, which is why losing the key means losing the data permanently and why a key kept with the machine removes the benefit entirely.

questions.explanation: Encrypted contents mean the drive reveals nothing wherever it goes, so disposal is safe as long as the key is out of reach. The same dependence on the key is why storing it with the machine removes the benefit.
questions.hint: Ask what the drive would reveal if it were read elsewhere.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where the recovery key changes the answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain the concern that follows when a recovery key is never reissued.

stimulus.body: An annotation on the survey sheet describes a recovery key that is generated once during enrolment and never changed afterwards. A note records that one of the people who held the key has left the organisation and that the key has not been reissued.

questions.stem: Given the annotation on the survey sheet, what concern follows from the key never being reissued?

options.text: The key will eventually expire on its own and stop granting access to the material
options.misconception: believes recovery keys expire automatically

options.text: The remaining holders will be unable to use the key because the departed holder was the custodian
options.misconception: thinks the key becomes unusable when a custodian leaves

options.text: A former holder retains the ability to recover the protected material for as long as it exists
The material will be unprotected once the departed holder account is closed
options.misconception: assumes closing the account revokes the key itself

questions.explanation: A key that is never reissued stays valid for whoever holds it, so a departed holder keeps a working path to the protected material. Revocation requires rotating the key, and that has not happened.
questions.hint: Ask whether the key was ever changed for the new holder.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the measured boot chain establishes
questions.learningObjective: State where a trusted reference value must be kept and how it is used.
questions.stem: Plate 52 of the field survey asks for two facts about a trusted reference value used in a measured boot chain.

options.text: It is stored where the measured images cannot reach it, and it is what the digest is compared to
It is stored where the measured images cannot reach it, and it is what the digest is compared against by the kernel
options.misconception: attaches the comparison to the kernel rather than to the boot measurement

options.text: It is stored on the measured disk so that it updates with each image, and it is what the digest is compared to
options.misconception: believes the reference lives on the same disk it protects

options.text: It is stored where the measured images cannot reach it, and it is regenerated at every boot by the firmware
options.misconception: thinks the reference is rebuilt at every startup

questions.explanation: The reference must sit outside the reach of the images it judges, otherwise an image and its reference could be swapped together. The boot measurement compares each digest with it first.
questions.hint: Ask where the expected value must be kept relative to the code.
